# SNP 1997 Manifesto Summary: "YES WE CAN - Win the Best for Scotland"

## Core Message

The 1997 SNP manifesto, introduced by Alex Salmond, presents Scottish independence as the essential solution to decades of neglect under Conservative and Labour governments. The central assertion is that Scotland—a wealthy nation contributing £27 billion more to London than it received since 1979—has been systematically held back by Westminster, and only independence can unlock Scotland's potential.

## The Case for Independence

The manifesto directly challenges "myths" about independence, asserting that Scotland would automatically become an EU member, maintain open borders with England, protect pensions and investments, and become one of Europe's wealthiest small nations. It emphasizes that nearly half of the world's most prosperous nations are small nations, positioning independence as the natural, proven path to prosperity.

## Route to Independence

An SNP parliamentary majority would trigger negotiations with Westminster and the EU, followed by a referendum on the "independence settlement." The process, estimated at 6-12 months, draws on precedents from nations that have achieved independence from Britain—none of which, the manifesto notes, sought to return to colonial status.

## Constitutional Vision

An independent Scotland would have a written constitution and Bill of Rights, establishing Scots as citizens rather than subjects. This includes a proportionally-elected single-chamber parliament, voting rights from age 16, constitutional protections for local government, and reform of the monarchy. The House of Lords would be replaced by transparent committee scrutiny.

## Economic Programme

The manifesto presents a fully-costed four-year budget projecting 100,000 new jobs, significant business tax reductions (corporation tax cut from 33% to 30%), and fair personal taxation where 85% of male and 95% of female employees would pay less tax. Progressive measures include removing the National Insurance ceiling for higher earners while introducing a starter income tax rate of 15%. The SNP pledges to reduce VAT on domestic fuel and begin repaying Scotland's inherited share of UK national debt.

## Social Justice Priorities

Key commitments include restoring an integrated NHS free from internal markets, increasing Child Benefit to £12.50 weekly, restoring benefits for 16-17 year olds, and introducing a "Pensioners Package" with increased state pensions, a Cold Climate Allowance, and abolished means-testing for elderly care. The minimum wage and EU Social Chapter would be adopted.

## Education and Housing

Education receives substantial focus: 700 additional teachers, free nursery provision for 3-4 year olds, abolition of student loans in favour of grants, and universal school internet access. Housing policy centres on transferring 75% of local authority housing debt to central government, releasing £1.6 billion to build 20,000 homes and eliminate homelessness.

## Rural Scotland and Environment

Agricultural policy emphasizes direct EU representation for Scottish farmers (denied under Westminster), reformed CAP support, and restoration of reputation following the BSE crisis through rigorous food safety. Fishing communities would benefit from regional management councils and enhanced structural support. Land reform through abolition of feudal tenure represents a fundamental commitment.

## Energy and Transport

Scotland's energy wealth—with 90% of North Sea output under Scottish jurisdiction—would be sustainably managed. Nuclear power would be phased out, replaced by renewable energy development at Dounreay. Transport investment includes public ownership of Railtrack, removal of Skye Bridge tolls, and integrated public transport networks.

## International Position

Independence would bring full EU membership with voting rights, doubled European Parliament representation, UN membership, and participation in Commonwealth and European institutions. A modern Scottish Defence Force would replace Trident nuclear weapons—negotiating NATO withdrawal while maintaining European security partnerships and establishing a peacekeeping college.

## Conclusion

The manifesto concludes that independence, backed by detailed financial planning, represents not separation but Scotland joining the community of normal, self-governing nations. The confident refrain—"YES WE CAN"—captures the SNP's fundamental argument: that Scottish wealth, talent, and resources are sufficient for independence, and only the political will to vote for it is required.
